Daily drill

One decision at a time.

Read the board, commit to a line, then compare it with the reasoning.

TODAY'S PUZZLE

Protect the threat or hold up interaction?

You40 life. Four untapped mana. One card in hand: a protection spell.
Your boardYour commander plus a value engine that will draw two cards on your next turn.
OpponentThree cards in hand, five untapped mana, and no profitable attack.

Your main phase: Do you add another threat or pass with protection available?

Pass with protection available.

You are already ahead on board and cards. Adding another permanent increases your exposure to a sweeper without materially improving your clock. Protect the engine, make the opponent act first, and spend mana only if they force you to.

STRATEGY NOTE

The question before every spell

What changes if this resolves?A spell that does not improve your clock, answer a threat, or increase future options may not be worth the mana now.
What am I exposing?Committing another card can turn an opponent's single answer into a two-for-one.
Who benefits from waiting?If your board already wins the long game, make the opponent break the tension.

Reality Fracture Draft Guide

FRA · Booster Draft

Set Overview

Reality Fracture (FRA) is the Echoverse draft environment, built around Jace Beleren’s mirror-multiverse story. Jace Beleren, now calling himself The Theorist, built a mirror multiverse: the Echoverse, a "what if" reconstruction of everything he judged worthy of keeping.

For draft, that story becomes a structural twist: every Play Booster contains three cards from the set's echoed pairs — legendary characters and their mirror-universe counterparts. Two of the three form a true pair (two Chandras, two Garruks); the third is unpaired. It makes every draft less predictable and every pack a small story.

270cards in main set
10draft archetypes
5Hexhaven colleges (allied pairs)
5character decks (enemy pairs)

The format is interactive by design: plentiful removal, common dual lands, and cheap spells. You rarely need to lock into a plan before you sit down — draft your two best colors and follow the signposts.

Mechanics

Empower Jace — the set's signature mechanic

Think "planeswalker amass." Empower Jace N puts N loyalty counters on a blue Jace planeswalker token you control — or creates one first if you don't have one. The token has −1: Surveil 1 and −3: Draw a card.

Empower appears at common in all five colors, and every source feeds one shared Jace token — so unrelated cards combine into real card advantage. Key play patterns from Draftsim's Day 0 guide:

  • When in doubt, −3 your Jace. Don't let loyalty pile up with no plan; convert it to cards.
  • Attack opposing Jaces early. A Jace left alone for four turns draws four cards. Kill it.
  • Don't overprotect your own Jace — losing it usually just costs you a card, not the game.
  • The ten "Way of the Planeswalker" uncommon enchantments each empower Jace on entry, then grant planeswalkers a new loyalty ability. Standouts: Way of the Cryomancer (copy a spell), Way of the Deathbringer (sacrifice value), Way of the Wildspeaker (immediate 4/4).
Prepare — creatures with a spell attached

Certain creatures enter prepared with an instant or sorcery "on their other half." While prepared, you may cast a copy of that spell — doing so unprepares the creature. Three allied-hybrid creatures re-prepare every upkeep, giving you a free spell per turn. Removal that answers the creature also answers the engine.

Surveil — look, then maybe bin

Look at the top card(s) of your library; put any number into your graveyard, the rest back on top. The WU Fatehold college turns surveil into aggression — creatures that grow or unlock when you've surveilled that turn.

Threshold — seven cards in your graveyard

The returning keyword: bonuses switch on with 7+ cards in your graveyard. The UB Theorix college is built around self-mill to hit threshold fast. Count your yard, not your hopes.

Flashback — second chances

Scattered across colors, mostly on value spells. Gives grindy decks inevitability and fuels threshold/delve-style graveyard counts.

Echoed Pairs & Pack Structure

Each Play Booster has three echoed-pair-slot cards: two form a true pair (same character, two versions), one is unpaired. Why it matters for draft:

  • Free information. If your opponent plays Chandra, Chill of Compliance, there's a real chance Chandra, Torch of Defiance was in the same pack pool. Sweat the mirror.
  • Pairs don't always pair well. Mabel, Bitter Recluse and Mabel, Valley Hero demand three colors with zero synergy. Don't force a pair that fights your deck.
  • Less predictability. Because one slot is unpaired, you can't reverse-engineer picks from a missing pair card the way you could if every pack were perfectly paired.

Notable echoed pairs to know on sight: the two Chandras (red planeswalker / blue planeswalker), the two Garruks (black / green planeswalkers), the two Lyras (blue / white angels), the two Ghaltas (white / green dinosaurs), and the uncommon Marwyns.

The 10 Draft Archetypes

Five allied pairs are Hexhaven's colleges (deeper synergy, each with a signature prepared spell). Five enemy pairs are character decks (more traditional strategies). All ten want Empower Jace cards — they're effectively colorless value.

The Five Colleges (allied)

Fatehold (WU) — Surveil aggro

Gameplan: Not Azorius control — this is tempo-aggression. Surveil to smooth draws while turning it into pressure via creatures that reward looking at your library.

Key cards: Desperate Futurescribe (signpost), Surveillance Phantasm, Prudent Fateseer, Proft Consulting Detective, Fatehold Charm.

Mirror-pair note: Denzilore Fatehold is the UW Elder Sphinx — a flash threat that snowballs on scry/surveil.

Draft tip: Prioritize efficient creatures over pure scry effects. A surveil that doesn't affect the board doesn't win games.

Theorix (UB) — Graveyard value / Threshold

Gameplan: Self-mill to seven cards, then turn on threshold payoffs. The college's mill-three prepared spell does double duty: affects the board while filling the yard.

Key cards: Recursive Recruitment (signpost), Theorix Charm, Paradox Shaper, Void Extrapolator, Proft Sinister Mastermind, Uldaros Theorix.

Draft tip: Never load up on payoffs without enablers. A threshold reward that's offline until turn nine is a dead card.

Stingerquill (BR) — Burn aggro

Gameplan: The most straightforward aggro pair. Noncombat damage triggers payoffs; removal doubles as synergy.

Key cards: Grim Repriser (signpost), Stingerquill Charm, Whiplash Wordsmith, Massacre Girl Most Wanted, No Admittance, Tomik Izzet Sparkmage.

Draft tip: Black has the fewest two-drops at common — prioritize early plays or you'll stumble out of the gate.

Konstrari (RG) — Heartwood ramp

Gameplan: Make Heartwood artifact tokens (tap for R/G), pour mana into expensive threats. Highest curve in the set — basic landcycling on big commons keeps it functional.

Key cards: Craftwork Crusher (signpost), Woodwork Prodigy, Heartwood Crafter, Konstrari Charm, Aerid Konstrari.

Draft tip: Don't skimp on ramp to jam more haymakers. The deck fails when it can't cast its spells on time.

Vigorbloom (GW) — Lifegain + counters

Gameplan: Lifegain isn't defensive here — it's a trigger. Bloombrute draws cards, Lyra grows angels, Kwia makes Lotus tokens.

Key cards: Bloombrute (signpost), Vigorbloom Charm, Vigorbloom Vanguard, Greenhouse Propagator, Kwia Vigorbloom.

Draft tip: Balance enablers with payoffs. Incidental lifegain on cards you'd play anyway beats dedicated gain-life spells.

The Five Character Decks (enemy)

Liliana's Attrition (WB) — Sacrifice midrange

Gameplan: Grindy Orzhov: lifegain plus sacrifice outlets, reanimation, and attrition. Draft bodies that are happy to trade, then pick up death triggers.

Key cards: Twisted Fates (signpost), Edgar Ancient Bloodlord, Way of the Deathbringer, Winter Tormented Loner.

Chandra's Prowess (UR) — Spells matter

Gameplan: Classic Izzet: burn + card selection + prowess threats. Run removal you'd play anyway — don't pad with mediocre tricks just for spell count.

Key cards: Clash of Elements (signpost), Saheeli Jewel of Avishkar, Stingcaster Mage, Chandra's Emberling, Tomik Izzet Sparkmage.

Draft tip: Keep answers for the late game. This deck runs out of gas against stalls.

Garruk's Bestiary (BG) — Value creatures

Gameplan: Golgari creatures that generate advantage entering and leaving. Graveyard recursion keeps the value flowing.

Key cards: Primal Witchstalker (signpost), Hapatra the Desert Fang, Vraska the Cutting Glare, Ferocity of the Hunt.

Ajani's Army (RW) — Counters aggro

Gameplan: Aggressive Boros on +1/+1 counters. Make 2/2 Cadet tokens, then buff them. Without counter payoffs it's just a burn shell.

Key cards: Warrior's Blades (signpost), Mabel Valley Hero, Yoshimaru Beloved Companion, Charge the Sanctum.

Jace's Mastery (UG) — Empower Jace control

Gameplan: The deepest planeswalker support: Mind Meanderer, Kiora of Salt and Sand, Tam's Resistance all want the biggest Jace possible.

Key cards: Mind Meanderer (signpost), Avatar of Burgeoning Echoes, Way of the Wildspeaker, Way of the Paradox.

Draft tip: Slowest lane and short on removal — treat as a trap unless pieces come late. The Jace enablers still go in any deck.

Draft Strategy

Pick order fundamentals

  1. Bomb rare/mythic that wins games alone (the S and A grades above).
  2. Premium removal — black is deepest (Last Gasp, Extended Absence, Vraska's Final Mercy); red has burn (No Admittance, Wrath of the Bloodmane).
  3. Empower Jace cards — they go in everything and stack onto one token.
  4. Efficient creatures for your archetype's curve.
  5. Fixing — the rare duals enter untapped with 2+ other lands; the common Annex duals need a planeswalker (your Jace token counts!).

When to commit

Stay open through pack one. The format's depth of playables means the correct two colors often reveal themselves in pack two. Commit when you see a signpost uncommon wheeling or a second premium card in the same pair.

Splashing

The common duals and Jace-token fixing make light splashes easy — but only for true bombs. Don't splash a B-grade card and wreck your mana.

Mana base

40-card draft decks: 16–17 lands for most curves, 18 for Konstrari-style ramp. Prioritize the rare duals; the Annex commons are fine as 23rd-land equivalents in Jace decks.

Tips & Traps

Common mistakes

  • Ignoring enemy Jace tokens. Four unanswered turns = four extra cards. Attack them early.
  • Overloading on threshold payoffs without mill enablers in UB.
  • Forcing echoed pairs that share nothing but a name (the Mabels, the Edgars).
  • Splashing B-grades and breaking your mana for a medium card.
  • Playing draw-go in WU. Fatehold is aggro — curve out.
  • Letting Jace loyalty pile up with no plan; convert to cards.

Overrated

  • Ingris Stingerquill — a 1/4 flyer for 3 that pings for 1. The GitHub analysis flagged it; believe it.
  • Way of the Mentor / Way of the Necromancer — the payoffs fight what your deck wants to do (Draftsim).
  • Yargle, Glutton of Urborg — 9 power that dies to a stiff breeze.
  • Omnipresence — 8-mana win-more.

Underrated

  • Empower Jace commons — they look unexciting; they quietly draw you three extra cards a game.
  • Way of the Cryomancer — copying a removal or draw spell breaks games open.
  • Basic landcycling on big commons — smooths the worst draws in ramp decks.
  • Prepared creatures — a free spell every turn warps combat math; kill them on sight.

Star Trek Draft Guide

TRK · Spoiler season — building
Contents Set Overview Mechanics Factions & Types Early Archetype Reads First-Look Watchlist Classified Card Review Commander Decks Road to Release Sources

Set Overview

Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek (TRK) is the next Universes Beyond release and the last big set of 2026 — a full-size, draftable expansion built for Star Trek's 60th anniversary (The Original Series premiered September 8, 1966). Lead designer Gavin Verhey's team pulled from the whole franchise: the original series, The Next Generation, Deep Space Nine, Voyager, and the newer shows all show up, tied together the way Trek always ties its eras together — time travel.

This guide is a spoiler-season build. The full preview season doesn't start until late October, so what follows is everything officially revealed so far — the First Look from July 14, 2026 — with early analysis clearly marked as early. Structure, mechanics reads, and the card watchlist will grow as previews land, and the tier-classified set review (Direct / Static / Engine, like Reality Fracture's) is live below in spoiler-season form — it fills out to the complete card list as previews land.

280cards in main set
Nov 132026 paper release
Nov 6–12prerelease week
4new mechanics

The confirmed headline cards so far are exactly who you'd want: Captain Kirk and Captain Kathryn Janeway (both also getting actor-signed headliner versions — William Shatner and Kate Mulgrew, roughly 200 copies each, Collector Booster only), the Borg Queen, Seven of Nine, Spock, and Chancellor Gowron. Treatments include an LCARS frame (29 cards, plus all 10 shock lands in LCARS) and a retro movie-poster "Enterprise" frame.

Mechanics

Assimilate — the Borg mechanic

Assimilating a creature means taking control of it — and improving it, Borg-style: it gains a +1/+1 counter, becomes an artifact creature, and becomes a Borg. This is theft that sticks and upgrades what it steals, which makes it the set's scariest late-game mechanic on paper: every creature you play is a potential future Borg. Anchored by Borg Queen, Perfection Manifest. Expect the Borg theme to play like Slivers do — artifact creatures that care about each other — so artifact synergies and animate-artifact effects get better the more Borg are around.

Face a Dilemma — modes matter

You "face a dilemma" whenever you choose one or more modes on a spell or ability — charms, commands, confluences, modal removal. Cards in the set pay you for doing it: Seven of Nine (a 2/4) draws you a card whenever you face a dilemma. The big deal: this isn't a closed mechanic. Thirty-plus years of existing modal cards face dilemmas too, so the payoff cards reach backward into Magic's whole history — in eternal formats, every charm in your deck is also a cantrip engine with Seven on the board. In Limited, it means modal spells punch above their rate whenever a dilemma payoff is in play.

Federation — creature types matter

An ability word for effects that scale with the number of creature types among non-Borg creatures you control. Hoshi Sato, Exolinguist shows the shape: when she enters, look at the top X cards of your library, where X is that type count — take one into hand, the rest go to the bottom. Federation rewards diverse crews: every distinct species and job on your side of the board deepens the dig. Changelings are the obvious force multiplier, and in draft it pushes you toward spreading creature types instead of doubling up.

Station & Spacecraft — returning from Edge of Eternities

Starships are Spacecraft with the station mechanic: they enter as artifacts, and you tap your creatures to add charge counters equal to their power until the ship powers up into a creature. U.S.S. Enterprise-D, Galaxy-Class is the flagship example. Station rewards wide boards and cheap creatures with real power — your crew literally crews the ship. Ships are slow to launch but enormous once online, so expect station density to define how aggressive the format can afford to be.

Cameos so far — explore and more

Captain Kathryn Janeway carries explore, fitting Voyager's whole deal. Wizards has said more returning mechanics will surface as previews continue — this section grows through spoiler season.

Factions & Types

The set's typal map is faction-first rather than college-first. Confirmed creature types and themes to plan around:

  • Borg — artifact creatures with a Sliver-like web of mutual support, built around assimilate and +1/+1 counters.
  • Klingon — the red aggro faction; expect battle cry-style wide aggression (the Commander deck leans this way too).
  • Vulcan — logic and choice; Spock, Logical Choice headlines the type.
  • Romulan — combat expertise under the microscope; watch this space in previews.
  • Officer — a new job type distinct from Soldier: Starfleet ranks matter, and officers recur across every crew.
  • Planet — a new token land that taps for any color; worlds you discover become mana.

Early Archetype Reads

The ten two-color draft archetypes haven't been officially published yet — they land with the full preview season in late October. What's below is the honest early map: the themes the revealed mechanics point at, so you know what to watch for when archetypes are announced. Nothing here is a guess dressed up as fact.

  • Borg counters / artifacts — assimilate plus artifact-creature payoffs. If the signpost uncommon is a Borg lord, this is the set's synergy-deep archetype.
  • Dilemma / modal spells — a spells deck that runs charms and modal removal because the payoffs (Seven of Nine and friends) refund them in cards.
  • Federation typal — go-wide with mixed creature types; the better your crew diversity, the deeper your card selection digs.
  • Station / spacecraft — crew up big ships; cheap high-power creatures do double duty as attackers and charge counters.
  • Klingon aggro — red-based aggression is all but confirmed by type and by the Klingon Fury deck's stated game plan.
  • Lifegain counters — Dr. Beverly Crusher grows whenever you gain life and doubles up lifegain triggers; Brad Boimler, Eager Ensign (2/2 lifelink) adds bonus counters whenever he's tapped. Two spoiled white cards pointing at the same deck is a signal, not a coincidence.

First-Look Watchlist

The spoiled cards with the most format gravity so far. Provisional grades for every spoiled card are live in the classified review below — they firm up as the pool fills out toward November.

1
Borg Queen, Perfection Manifest
Legendary — Borg · Assimilate anchor

The mechanic's flagship. If assimilate is costed aggressively anywhere, it's here — and every stolen creature coming back bigger, artifact-typed, and Borg-typed means she snowballs boards that were beating you a turn ago.

2
Seven of Nine
Legendary — 2/4 · Dilemma payoff

Draw a card whenever you face a dilemma. In Limited that's a reason to pick modal spells early; everywhere else, she turns three decades of charms and commands into card advantage.

3
Khan, Engineered Evil
Bonus sheet · Sheoldred, the Apocalypse reskin

Not Standard-legal and not part of the draft environment — it's Sheoldred wearing a Khan skin, in Play and Collector Boosters. Sheoldred needs no introduction; expect this to be a chase card on name alone.

4
U.S.S. Enterprise-D, Galaxy-Class
Spacecraft · Station

The face of the station mechanic. How fast the D comes online relative to its payoff decides whether spacecraft are a real draft pillar or a splashy trap — the single most important rate to learn at prerelease.

5
Dr. Beverly Crusher + Brad Boimler, Eager Ensign
White · Lifegain / counters pair

Crusher gains a counter whenever you gain life and doubles lifegain triggers; Boimler adds extra counters while tapped. Together they're the clearest two-card archetype signal of the First Look.

6
The City on the Edge of Forever
Saga

An iconic episode told in saga chapters — the set's storytelling swing. Sagas have a strong recent hit rate in Limited; full text lands in preview season.

Also confirmed and worth tracking: Captain Kirk, Boldly Going, Captain Kathryn Janeway (explore), Spock, Logical Choice, Chancellor Gowron, Crystalline Entity, Hoshi Sato, Exolinguist, Warp Speed, and — confirmed by the design team — Tribbles, multiplying exactly as fast as you'd fear.

Commander Decks (TRC)

Four three-color decks accompany the set (all four include white). Commander product lives in the MTG Hub — this is the competitive-relevant summary only:

  • Federation Fleet — card draw and charging starships.
  • Klingon Fury — aggression that hits the whole battlefield.
  • Landing Party — explore and landfall, led by Spock.
  • We Are the Borg — grow the ranks and assimilate the enemy, led by the Borg Queen.

Each deck carries 33 new-to-Magic cards. A Collector's Edition (all Surge Foil) also exists at $159.99.

Road to Release

  • July 14, 2026 — First Look: mechanics, headline legends, treatments revealed. (Done — this guide is built from it.)

  • Early November 2026 — full card gallery; the spoiler-season classified review below fills out to the complete pool and grades firm up.
  • November 6–12, 2026 — prerelease week at local stores.
  • November 10, 2026 — Arena release.

Puzzles

Three ways to think

Make the call.

Read each position, choose your line, then reveal the answer and reasoning.

ROLE ASSIGNMENT

Which player is the beatdown?

You28 life, four medium creatures, no cards in hand.
Opponent12 life, two blockers, five cards in hand, and the stronger late game.
Your drawA flexible removal spell that can clear one blocker.

Your decision: Save removal for a future bomb, or clear a blocker and attack now?

Clear the blocker and press the attack.

Your opponent has more cards and inevitability. Saving the removal gives them time to turn those cards into a winning board. Your role is the beatdown, so convert the spell into damage while your battlefield advantage still matters.

COMBAT MATH

Find the winning attack.

YouAt 6 life with a 5/5 trampler, two 3/3s, and a 2/2.
OpponentAt 9 life with a 4/4 and a 2/2 available to block.
Your handA spell that gives one creature +3/+0 after blockers.

Your decision: Which creatures attack, and where does the pump go?

Attack with everything. Pump an unblocked attacker.

The toughest blocks put the 4/4 on your trampler and the 2/2 on a 3/3. One trample damage, an unblocked 3/3, the 2/2, and the +3/+0 add to exactly 9. Any other blocks let through at least that much.

MULLIGAN

Keep seven or ship it?

Opening handTwo lands (one enters tapped), a 2-drop, a 3-drop, a 5-drop, and two 6-drops.
CommanderCosts four mana.
On the playNo free draw before your second turn.

Your decision: Keep or mulligan?

Mulligan.

The tapped land pushes the 2-drop to turn three, and half the hand cannot be cast without several perfect draws. A coherent six with three lands and a curve is stronger than seven cards that do not function together.

Draft 3 — Paper Night at Cardtropolis + the Sim Lab

Oct 16–17, 2026

2–1 in paper against real draft pools; 43.6% in the lab against the format's best trophy decks. A genuinely competitive deck — it beats the tempo, Gruul, and Dimir trophies — but it needs the play, and its sim percentages are likely understated: the pilot caveat below cuts hardest on exactly this kind of deck.

2–1Paper record · games 5–3
218–282Sims vs trophy decks · 43.6% · 500 games
50% / 37%On the play / on the draw

The night (paper)

Wes's third Reality Fracture draft — FNM at Cardtropolis TCG, Silverdale — played exactly as built: a Jeskai deck, white-blue splashing red (6 Plains, 6 Island, 2 Mountains plus duals), with Tomik, Chandra's Emberling, and Infinite Coursework in the final 40.

OpponentMatchGames
Dan2–1Win – loss – win
Trevor2–0Win – win
Holly1–2Loss – win – loss
  • Hasty early, sharp late. He played hastily in the first two matches and missed obvious plays, then slowed down and sequenced properly by the third.
  • Set Review paid off against Holly. Knowing Blazing Crescendo was red's only pump trick let him take near-lethal damage and swing back for his one game off her.
  • Game 3 vs Holly: lost with Sphinx of False Conclusions stranded in hand — eight lands, but only one blue source.
  • Against Trevor, an inexperienced opponent left his Jace token alone all game, and Wes surveilled off it repeatedly.
  • The format lesson: Trevor's mid-game turn spent entirely on a vanilla Wrecking Gecko — answered next turn by Infinite Coursework. In a set full of enters-the-battlefield effects, a do-nothing body is a wasted turn.

The sims

The morning after, the same 40 cards were run in FRAE (Rowan's engine; heuristic pilot in both seats, 50 games per matchup, alternating play/draw) against 10 real trophy decks pulled from 17Lands — the best 7-x list for each top color identity in Reality Fracture Premier Draft. Scores are Wes's deck first:

Trophy deckRecordWin %
UR — tempo38–1276%
RG — Gruul31–1962%
UB — Dimir26–2452%
UBG23–2746%
WUB22–2844%
WUb19–3138%
BG18–3236%
WU17–3334%
BR15–3530%
WG — go-wide Selesnya9–4118%
Total — 500 games218–28243.6%
  • Genuinely competitive with real top-end draft pools — it beats the tempo, Gruul, and Dimir trophies — but it is a below-.500 deck against trophy-caliber opposition under this pilot.
  • Worst matchup: go-wide Selesnya (18%). And the WU trophy is a better version of its own plan.
  • The deck needs the play. The play/draw split persists against real decks: 50% on the play, 37% on the draw.
  • The harsher stress test: against synthetic archetype best-builds (best possible lists with duplicated bombs) it scored 119–381 (23.8%) — those games drag to 16–17 turns and the deck loses the long game. That opponent set was superseded by the trophy decks, which answer the question actually asked.
  • Calibration benchmark: the same engine rates Wes's Oct 15 deck at 46% against the Azorius best-build, where Draft 3 scored 10% — the instrument ranks Draft 3 well below the Oct 15 deck. Direction is informative; absolute percentages are not store predictions.
Caveats — load-bearing

The FRAE pilot failed its Gate 2 head-to-head (0.475 against the Forge AI): it extracts fewer wins from the same lists, worst in sequencing-heavy shells — and Draft 3 is the most sequencing-dependent deck yet simmed, so its percentages are likely understated more than a simple deck's. Equal-pilot deck-vs-deck differences are the trustworthy output, not absolute win rates. Trophy decks are the top of the format, not a typical FNM pod — the paper result (2–1) came against real draft pools.

Engine note: this study caught and fixed two engine crashes (a prepared-spell cast crash and a damage-effect argument bug); the K1 decision battery re-verified 6/6 families after each fix.

Monte Carlo

Oct 15, 2026

Your Oct 15 red-white Reality Fracture draft deck, simulated against top-decile builds of the format's three best archetypes — 10 games per matchup, in both the Living Library build and the Teyo build. The Library build out-records the Teyo build — and the mechanism data below explains why.

17–13 · 57%Living Library build · 30 games
16–14 · 53%Teyo build · 30 games
0Teyo saves in 30 games

At population level (17Lands, ~515K Premier Draft games), Azorius wins 57.2%, Izzet 56.1%, and Gruul 56.0%; Boros sits at 54.1% — so these were uphill fights by design.

MatchupLibrary buildTeyo build
vs Azorius (WU) Empower Control5–55–5
vs Izzet (UR) Prowess Tempo7–37–3
vs Gruul (RG) Stompy Aggro5–54–6
Total — 30 games each17–13 (57%)16–14 (53%)

The verdicts

  • Library stays in. The Library build out-recorded the Teyo build, and the mechanism explains why (below).
  • Teyo recorded zero saves in 30 games. Removal was aimed at your creatures 20 times; Teyo was in hand for about 4 of those, and in none of them was {1}{W} actually open — the deck taps out curving out, and its white spells spend the white mana. His realized value was late flash-ins as a 1/1 with a counter.
  • The card-draw gap is real. Your deck drew ~0.43 extra cards per game (all from Blazing Crescendo impulse); opponents drew ~2.3 extra per game from draw spells and planeswalker value.

Mechanism diagnostics

  • Vicious Verse is a real engine — the prepared spell was cast ~20 times per 30 games, a recurring ping that keeps coming back.
  • Living Library's {6} tuck fired only twice in its 30 games — it's insurance, not a plan.
  • Empower pressure is real but not dominant: opponents held a planeswalker for roughly one turn per game on average.
  • Biggest loss tag: “run over fast” — 5 of the Library build's 13 losses, 8 of the Teyo build's 14. Then flood (4 each) and being outvalued on cards.
  • Average game length ~8 rounds. No ties. Small sample — treat the mechanisms as the findings, not the exact records.

The research program

The simplified Monte Carlo above was the scout. The lab engine is now FRAE, Rowan's homegrown Reality Fracture engine (Forge was retired as a pilot after its AI's biases distorted results; it remains only as a rules oracle). FRAE passed its rules-accuracy and speed gates, but its pilot lost the Gate 2 head-to-head (0.475), so every sim verdict on this page carries the pilot caveat: trust deck-vs-deck differences, not absolute win rates. The standing sample bar for any verdict is 200+ games per pairing, aimed at mechanic interactions, hidden archetypes, card re-evaluation against guide grades, and play patterns — with the lessons taught back here.

Caveats

Small sample — 10 games per matchup per build, 60 games total, on a simplified Monte Carlo engine. Treat the mechanisms as the findings, not the exact records.

Monte Carlo Study — Your Oct 15 R/W Draft DeckLibrary vs Teyo across 60 games against the format's three best archetypes.
Complete

Monte Carlo Study — Your Oct 15 R/W Draft Deck

CompleteOct 15, 202660 games · 30 per buildSimplified Monte Carlo engine

The rundown

  • Library stays in. The Living Library build went 17–13 (57%); the Teyo build went 16–14 (53%) — and the mechanism data explains the gap, not just the record.
  • Teyo recorded zero saves in 30 games. His protection mode never once had the mana and the moment line up.
  • The card-draw gap is the deck's real problem: ~0.43 extra cards per game for you vs ~2.3 per game for opponents.
  • Biggest loss tag: “run over fast” — the deck's losses are about early pressure more than late-game value.
60games simulated
2builds tested head-to-head
3top archetypes faced
~8rounds per game, average
Matchup Results17–13 Library · 16–14 Teyo

Ten games per matchup, per build, against top-decile builds of the format's three best archetypes. At population level (17Lands, ~515K Premier Draft games), Azorius wins 57.2%, Izzet 56.1%, and Gruul 56.0%, while Boros sits at 54.1% — so these were uphill fights by design.

MatchupLibrary buildTeyo build
vs Azorius (WU) Empower Control5–55–5
vs Izzet (UR) Prowess Tempo7–37–3
vs Gruul (RG) Stompy Aggro5–54–6
Total — 30 games each17–13 (57%)16–14 (53%)
Per-matchup notes
  • Azorius (5–5 / 5–5): Dead even in both builds. The empower-control deck is the format's population leader, so parity here is a respectable result — the matchup turns on card quantity, which is where the draw gap (below) bites hardest.
  • Izzet (7–3 / 7–3): The best matchup for both builds. The R/W deck races the prowess tempo plan effectively and its removal lines up well.
  • Gruul (5–5 / 4–6): The one matchup where the builds separate. The Teyo build dropped a game the Library build didn't — consistent with the loss tags, where the Teyo build was run over more often.
Deck Verdict — Library vs TeyoLibrary stays in
  • Library stays in. It out-recorded the Teyo build overall and in the Gruul matchup, and unlike Teyo it at least carries a late-game button (below).
  • Teyo's realized value was tiny: across 30 games his appearances amounted to late flash-ins as a 1/1 with a counter — a mediocre creature, not the protection piece he was slotted as.
Why Teyo recorded zero saves
  • Opponent removal was aimed at your creatures 20 times across the 30 games — the opportunities existed.
  • Teyo was actually in hand for only about 4 of those moments.
  • In none of them was {1}{W} actually open: the deck taps out curving out, and its white spells spend the white mana his flash-protection mode needs.
  • The lesson generalizes: a reactive card in a deck that never holds mana up is a card that never fires. The slot has to match how the deck actually plays its turns.
Card & Mechanism EvidenceWhat actually did the work
  • Vicious Verse is a real engine — Voxmancer's prepared spell was cast ~20 times per 30 games, a recurring ping that keeps coming back. One card, repeatedly producing spells: prepared is static card advantage in practice.
  • Living Library's {6} tuck fired only twice in its 30 games — it's insurance, not a plan. The card earns its slot on its body and flexibility, not on the activated ability.
  • Empower pressure is real but not dominant: opponents held a planeswalker for roughly one turn per game on average.
The card-draw gap, in detail
  • Your deck drew ~0.43 extra cards per game — and all of it came from Blazing Crescendo's impulse draw.
  • Opponents drew ~2.3 extra cards per game from draw spells and planeswalker value.
  • That's roughly a two-card-per-game deficit against decks built on the format's advantage engines — the single clearest structural weakness the study found, and the thing to draft around next time: empower sources and prepared spells are advantage too, even though they never say “draw a card.”
Loss Analysis“Run over fast” leads both builds
  • Run over fast: 5 of the Library build's 13 losses, 8 of the Teyo build's 14 — the dominant tag in both, and worse in the build with the reactive card that never fired.
  • Flood: 4 losses in each build — a real but secondary factor, roughly what you'd expect from variance across 30 games.
  • Outvalued on cards: the remainder — the slow losses, where the draw gap compounds turn over turn.
What the loss tags mean for the next draft

Two of the three loss causes are draft-addressable: cheap early interaction and real advantage sources (empower, prepared) attack both “run over fast” and “outvalued.” Flood is mostly variance — noted, not chased. The Teyo experiment adds a deckbuilding rule: don't slot reactive protection into a curve-out deck and expect saves.

Method & CaveatsSmall sample — mechanisms over records
  • Simplified Monte Carlo engine; 10 games per matchup per build, 60 games total. Average game length ~8 rounds, no ties.
  • At this sample size the exact records are soft — a game or two flips any single matchup line. Treat the mechanisms as the findings, not the exact records: cast counts, save opportunities, and draw totals are far more stable than a 17–13.
  • That caveat is exactly why the Forge program exists: the standing bar for any verdict there is 200+ games per pairing at full rules fidelity.

The PlanPrep → Play → Review → Drill

The loop

Prep→Play→Review→Drill

Every session runs the same shape: 15 min prep (one concept) → 60 min play → 15 min review log. Most players only play — the improvement lives in the other three steps. Stop after 2 straight tilt losses. No exceptions.

Split: 70% Limited / 30% Constructed + Brawl. Limited teaches card evaluation, curve, combat math, and deckbuilding from scratch — and builds the Arena collection. Brawl sharpens Commander instincts; Standard Bo3 is where sideboarding gets learned properly.

Phase 0 — Baseline · Oct 14–18, 2026

  • Play 3 Quick Drafts of Reality Fracture — no studying first, this is your natural game on record.
  • Pick ONE Brawl or Standard deck and stick with it for 30 games. No deck-hopping.
  • After each draft, note the record, your two colors and why you landed there, and the one moment you weren't sure what to do.
  • Record your starting Limited and Constructed ranks in Ranks & Goals below.

Phase 1 — Foundations · Oct 19 – Nov 9, 2026

  • Mon — Study (no games): set review + 17Lands top commons/uncommons, the 10 archetypes and signposts, then 20 picks in the Draft Quiz.
  • Tue — Draft: one full Premier/Quick Draft. Send the pool for cuts + curve review before playing it.
  • Wed — Constructed: ladder Bo3 with your one deck, working only the focus drill of the week.
  • Thu — Draft + Puzzles: one draft plus 3 combat puzzles from the Hub.
  • Fri — Review day (light play): revisit your 2 worst losses. What turn did it swing? What did open mana represent? Tag the leak.
  • Weekend: paper Commander counts — practice role assessment (who's the threat, who's the beatdown).

Weekly focus drills

  • Week 1 (Oct 19) — Mulligans: say out loud why every keep works — lands, a 2 and a 3, a plan.
  • Week 2 (Oct 26) — Combat: before attacking, name every profitable and unprofitable block they have.
  • Week 3 (Nov 2) — Open mana: before your main spell, name the removal or trick their colors could be holding.
  • Week 4 (Nov 9) — Sequencing: play lands and cheap spells in the order that keeps the most options open next turn.

Phase 2 — Level Up · Nov 10 – Dec 7, 2026

  • Move draft to Traditional Bo3 at least once a week — sideboarding in Limited is where good players pull away.
  • Sideboard maps: write your in/out for each major matchup before you look at a guide, then compare.
  • Targets by Dec 7: Platinum in Limited, Platinum in Constructed, draft win rate trending to 53–55%, one leak category clearly shrinking.

Phase 3 — Per-set cycle · after Dec 7, 2026

Repeat every new set: Week 1 sealed + set review + Quick Drafts to learn cards cheap, Weeks 2–4 Premier Drafts pushing rank, final week reviewing what the format taught you.

Arena economy rules

  • Wins first in training drafts — don't rare-draft. You're buying lessons, not cards.
  • Don't spend wildcards until Phase 2, and only on a deck you'll play 50+ games.

    Before you queue — 60-second check

    1. Name the likely field: roughly 3 in 5 opponents will be on one of the 10 above. Izzet Spellementals + Mono Green Landfall alone are ~22% combined.
    2. Check your sideboard covers the top 3 jobs: graveyard hate (Jund, Excruciator, Spellementals), a sweeper or cheap removal for go-wide / landfall, and a way to kill a planeswalker or enchantment (Kaito, Unholy Annex).
    3. Know your one must-answer card per matchup — it's called out in every “Beating it” box below.
    4. Don't over-board: most plans below swap 4–6 cards. Cutting your own engine to answer everything is how midrange decks beat themselves.
